to [**Hospital6 1597**] for a GI bleed.  She was brought to
the ER by EMS from Rehab.  The patient denied chest pain or
shortness of breath, complaining of abdominal pain for years
but has felt increased pain over the last few weeks.  The
patient is a rather poor historian.  The patient had her last
bowel movement the night before admission.  The patient was
sent to be evaluated for left lower quadrant tenderness due
to obstipation.  Recent barium enema 8 days ago (patient had
KUB at nursing home rehab) demonstrating barium obstipation.
At [**Hospital3 **] the patient underwent CT scanning.  A plain
film was performed.  There was free air on the film.  The
patient underwent a CT scan with no contrast in an attempt to
find a leak.  It was decided that the patient needed to have
urgent surgery and the patient was transferred to [**Hospital3 **]
[**Hospital **] [**First Name (Titles) **] [**Last Name (Titles) **] secondary to OR scheduling conflict.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:  CREST syndrome, history of upper GI
bleed, and GERD.

PAST SURGICAL HISTORY:  Transabdominal hysterectomy,
appendectomy.

MEDICATIONS AT HOME:  Ativan
Nexium
Procardia

ALLERGIES:  Penicillin.

HEALTH CARE PROXY:  Granddaughter.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:  The patient was alert and oriented
times three, in no acute distress.  Chest was clear to
auscultation, prolonged expiratory phase.  Abdomen revealed
right lower quadrant tenderness and guarding.

HOSPITAL COURSE:  On admission to [**Hospital1 18**], the patient was
taken directly to the operating room, where an exploratory
laparotomy was performed revealing ischemic colon.  The
patient underwent a colectomy and a Hartmann's procedure.
The patient also had gross fecal spillage in the abdomen.
The operation was relatively uneventful.  She did have
approximately 500 cc blood loss.

After surgery, the patient was admitted to Intensive Care
Unit for close observation.  She was intubated.  She was also
placed on Lopressor and her cardiac enzymes were cycled
secondary to concern about a cardiac event from labs at the
outside hospital.  The patient did have an NG tube in place
and was left NPO.  The patient showed postoperative oliguria,
which required bolusing to keep her urine output adequate.
The patient was placed on vancomycin, levofloxacin, Flagyl,
and fluconazole.  The patient had a right internal jugular,
right femoral arterial line, Foley, NG tube, ET tube in place
when she left the operating room.

The patient remained in the PACU on the first postoperative
night secondary to lack of beds in the ICU.  Her biggest
problem at that time was her urinary output.  On that day,
the patient received an echocardiogram, which revealed a 60
percent ejection fraction, and slight right ventricular
hypokinesis.  The following day, the patient self-extubated
herself.  As the patient was appearing to do fairly well,
this was a tolerated event and the patient remained extubated
and on high oxygen therapy.  The patient did have an issue
with atrial fibrillation postoperatively in the ICU initially
and this was treated with Lopressor and magnesium with little
effect.  The patient was finally placed on amiodarone drip
which was successful in keeping the patient in sinus rhythm.

On postoperative day three, the patient's respiratory status
began to worsen a little bit with pO2 persistently in the 60s
throughout the day.  The patient was, however, closely
watched for acute changes and frequently blood gases were
drawn as the patient suffered from CREST syndrome, which made
monitoring by pulse oximetry difficult.  It was decided
secondary to evaluating a chest x-ray that the patient was
probably in mild pulmonary edema.  The patient was diuresed
with Lasix.  The patient improved her pO2 slightly, but not
by any significant means.

Over the course of the day, the patient was very closely
followed, however at approximately 12:30 in the morning on
[**2161-7-19**], the patient had an acute drop in her pO2 to 40
percent.  She became acutely hypotensive with a very low
heart rate, which on EKG appeared to be a junctional rhythm.
The patient was placed on Levophed and neo-synephrine for
pressure control and the patient was ultimately reintubated.
However, upon reintubation, the patient did not experience an
improvement in her oxygenation; for this reason, the patient
was then changed to pressure control ventilation, still not
causing any improvement in her ventilation.  The patient had
a chest x-ray to confirm endotracheal tube placement, as well
as to evaluate pulmonary edema.  Pulmonary edema was
significantly worse though the ET tube was in place.

Due to the patient's failure to improve, the ICU attending on
call was called to the bedside for assistance.  It was
decided to paralyze Ms. [**Known lastname 174**] in an attempt to improve her
respiratory function, however this did not occur to any great
degree with paralytic.  Cardiology was called and
echocardiogram was performed at the bedside showing global
left ventricular dysfunction and ejection fraction of 20
percent, right ventricular hypokinesis, moderate tricuspid
regurgitation, mild mitral regurgitation.  The patient was
given 2 liters of normal saline, as well, to try and increase
her blood pressure.  Cor pulmonale was also ruled out on
echocardiogram, indicating that a large PE was probably not
to blame for the patient's problems.

Finally, despite being on Levophed and neo-synephrine, the
patient acutely dropped her pressure, which was refractory to
pressor administration.  The patient received boluses of
epinephrine as well as bicarbonate for her metabolic acidosis
that had developed.  This, however, was to no avail as the
patient finally expired at approximately 5:00 am on
[**2161-7-19**].

mcg/kg/min and weaning to a low of 7.5 mcg/kg/min.

with total fluids at 100 cc/kg/day.  Her dextrose sticks were
stable at 102 and 63.  At approximately eight to ten hours of
age she had her first void of 12 cc.  She had not passed any
meconium.

Hematology - The infant was given packed red blood cells at
20 cc/kg, divided in two aliquots.

Neurology - The infant did not survive long enough to receive
head ultrasound screening as well as audiology or
ophthalmology screening.  She was given Fentanyl for pain
control and sedation.

The Neonatal Team sat with the mother once the mother was
able to leave [**Hospital6 1597**] to visit Aniya.  She was
updated at the bedside by me and the medical team.  Mother
understood that we were unable to provide any other support
for Aniya and that the respiratory failure was likely due to
her extreme prematurity which again calculates to about 23
6/7 weeks.  Mother understood and support was withdrawn;
mother held her [**Known firstname **] girl in her arms.  Time of death was
16:58 PM.  Mother did have some family support at the
bedside.  She did decline any hospital pastoral services as
well as an autopsy.

FINAL DIAGNOSIS:
1.  Extreme prematurity.
2.  Respiratory distress syndrome.
3.  Rule out sepsis.
4.  Hypotension.
5.  Anemia.
6.  Metabolic acidosis.
